clue.text: Mate here, in more ways than one

definitions.text: Mate here, in more ways than one

parts.words: Mate here, in more ways than one
parts.note: a ship's mate works on a vessel, and checkmate happens on a chessboard, so both kinds of mate are found in this place

explanation.surface: Someone asks where a mate might be found, hinting at several kinds of mate.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's officer is aboard the vessel, and a chess mate takes place on the playing board, so the phrase fits both senses.

clue.text: Finished drink? Some coincidence!

parts.note: over means finished, as in the game is over
to lap is to drink as a cat does

explanation.surface: After the last drink someone remarks on a striking chance event.
explanation.definitionFit: Where two things overlap, they partly coincide or cover the same ground.

clue.text: Programme, so to speak

parts.note: a radio or television show, which is also a spreading of words widely, sown like seed thrown by hand

explanation.surface: A loose way of naming a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A transmitted radio or TV show, and the word also means spoken or scattered far and wide.

clue.text: Test matches — with this result?

parts.note: the England–Australia cricket Test series is named after a trophy urn, and burnt matchsticks leave this residue

explanation.surface: A question about how a cricket series might end.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test match is an international cricket game; England and Australia play for the Ashes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ashes is the England–Australia cricket Test series, and what remains after matches burn.

clue.text: Girl's put on garment to do stripping act

indicators.note: put on means the girl's name sits above the garment in this down entry

parts.note: Di is a short girl's name, and the possessive gives the s
a mantle is a loose cloak

explanation.surface: A woman dresses up in a cloak for a striptease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' stacks the pieces in this down entry; 'stripping act' suggests a striptease but means taking something apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle is to take something apart, stripping it down to its components.

clue.text: Dark soon, here in Ireland?

parts.note: a candle whose wick is low will soon go out and leave the room dark, and the phrase split that way names an Irish county

explanation.surface: A remark that night falls early in some part of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the county name as two words, a wick that is low, and darkness is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicklow is a county south of Dublin; split in two it describes a candle burnt down, promising darkness.

clue.text: Turned, roughly speaking, in part of South-East

indicators.note: roughly speaking says the word for turned is said aloud and only approximately matches

parts.note: a car or a flock of birds that turned has wheeled

explanation.surface: Someone changed direction while travelling in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: The Weald is a once-wooded area of Kent and Sussex in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Weald is a region of south-east England between the North and South Downs.

clue.text: Cosmetic best after infection

indicators.note: after places the word for best behind the word for infection

parts.note: a cold is a common viral infection
the cream is the best part, as in the cream of the crop

explanation.surface: Advice that a beauty product works best once you've had a bug.
explanation.definitionFit: An emollient used to cleanse and soften the skin.

clue.text: Crime as gunmen pinched from politician

indicators.note: pinched from means the gunners are stolen out of the word for politician

parts.note: a Liberal is a member of the Liberal Party
RA is the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners

explanation.surface: Armed robbers rob a politician in a criminal act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinched from' removes RA (Royal Artillery) from LIBERAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Defamation in writing, which can be a criminal offence.

clue.text: Erratic course over part of city

indicators.note: over means the word for course sits above the word for city district in this down entry

parts.note: a way is a route or course
a ward is an electoral division of a city

explanation.surface: An unsteady route across a district of town.
explanation.definitionFit: Wayward means unpredictable and wilful.

clue.text: After retreat, contend with hard time

indicators.note: a retreat goes backwards, so the word for contend is read in reverse

parts.note: to contend with something is to cope with it
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A soldier, having fallen back, must struggle through a difficult spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After retreat' reads the word for contend backwards (EPOC); 'retreat' looks like the past event the time follows, but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An epoch is an era or period, a span of history.

clue.text: Constant? One employed by trainer

parts.note: a steady, unchanging lad is a stable one, and a racehorse trainer employs a youngster to muck out the horses

explanation.surface: A question about a faithful employee of a coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trainer' suggests a gym or a shoe, but here it is a racehorse trainer.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing yard hires a lad to care for the horses, and the first half of the job title also means steady.

clue.text: Daily's mad, perhaps, to be a servant

indicators.note: perhaps shows these letters are only one possible arrangement, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: A cleaner has gone crazy and taken a job in service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges DAILYSMAD; 'Daily' looks like a newspaper or a cleaner, but it is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's personal attendant in a grand household is a female domestic helper.

clue.text: Essayist goes on about a girl

indicators.note: goes on means the essayist's name is placed after the letter for about

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
Elia was the pen name of the essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A writer drones on about some young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Elia was the pseudonym used by Charles Lamb for his essays; 'goes on' puts it after C.
explanation.definitionFit: Celia is a female first name.

clue.text: Joke makes little change to nobility

parts.note: P stands for penny, a small coin
rank means high social standing, as in persons of rank

explanation.surface: A wit says a small alteration to the aristocracy is laughable.
explanation.definitionFit: A prank is a practical trick played for fun.

clue.text: Demolish county after first innings

indicators.note: after puts the county name behind the cricket word

parts.note: in cricket a batsman's innings is called a knock, and it comes first here
Down is a county of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A county side collapses after an opening cricket innings.
explanation.walkthrough: A knock is a batsman's innings in cricket; Down is a county in Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock down a building is to raze it.

clue.text: A couple of dolts could be so trite

parts.note: a couple of times is twice

indicators.note: could be shows the letters of the word for fool may be rearranged

parts.note: a dolt is a fool; the plural comes from the couple, and each one gives the same four letters

explanation.surface: Two idiots might be described as dull and unoriginal.
explanation.walkthrough: Two dolts rearranged each make TOLD, so the phrase is TOLD twice; 'could be' signals the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A story repeated so often it has grown stale and hackneyed.

clue.text: Rebellious one demanding quick action about partners

indicators.note: about means the words for one and pressing go around the partners

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
something urgent needs prompt attention
North and South are partners at the bridge table

explanation.surface: An agitator demands swift action on behalf of colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: N and S, the bridge partners North and South, go inside I + URGENT, signalled by 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurgent describes someone rising in revolt against authority.

clue.text: Former bridge designer in court

parts.note: old means former, as in an old flame
Sir Donald Bailey designed the portable Bailey bridge used in WWII

explanation.surface: A retired engineer appears before a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Bailey is London's Central Criminal Court.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Bailey is the popular name for England's Central Criminal Court in London.

clue.text: Spaniard held back by the Irish supporter? Not he

indicators.note: held means the Spanish word is gripped inside the word for Irishmen

parts.note: Pat is a stock nickname for an Irishman, so the Irish are Pats

indicators.note: back means the Spanish word is read in reverse

parts.note: senor is the Spanish word for a man or gentleman

explanation.surface: A man from Spain is detained by the Irish, and his backer turns out to be a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' gives RONES, the Spanish word backwards; 'held' puts it inside the Irishmen. 'Not he' says the supporter is a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A female sponsor or benefactor of the arts or a charity.

clue.text: Lots of Constables, society means to have

parts.note: posses are bands of lawmen gathered together

explanation.surface: A collection of landscape paintings is something a society aims to own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constables' looks like the painter's works, but means police officers.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess something is to own or hold it.

clue.text: King writing about princess

indicators.note: about means the writing abbreviation goes around the princess

parts.note: MS is short for manuscript, a piece of writing
Princess Ida is the heroine of a Gilbert and Sullivan opera

explanation.surface: A monarch composes a piece about a royal daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the writing around the princess: Ida is the title heroine of Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera Princess Ida.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Phrygian monarch whose touch turned everything to gold.

clue.text: Top dog could be Pom? Sure

indicators.note: could be shows the letters given might form another word when rearranged

explanation.surface: An Australian wonders whether an Englishman might be the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: A Pom is Australian slang for an English person.
explanation.definitionFit: A supremo is the person in overall charge, the boss.

clue.text: Animate gallant young fellow.

explanation.surface: Bring a dashing youth to life.
explanation.definitionFit: To spark something is to set it going or enliven it, and a bright spark is a lively, dashing young man.

clue.text: Tailor gives a daughter fitting

parts.note: D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter
apt means suitable or fitting

explanation.surface: A dressmaker gives a girl a fitting session.
explanation.definitionFit: To tailor something is to alter it to suit a purpose.

clue.text: Eccentric's instrument for fiddler

parts.note: a card is an odd or amusing person, and the possessive gives the s
a harp is a stringed musical instrument

explanation.surface: An oddball owns something to be played by a violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddler' suggests a violinist, but here it means a cheat at cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler who cheats at card games, someone who fiddles.

clue.text: Move effortlessly along shore

explanation.surface: Glide easily by the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: To coast is to glide along without power, and the coast is the land by the sea.

clue.text: Witch gets one by replacing contents of spell

indicators.note: replacing contents means the inside of the word spell is swapped out, keeping its first and last letters

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sorceress gets someone to change what an incantation says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacing contents of' keeps S and L of 'spell' and puts IBY in place of PEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibyl was a prophetess of the ancient world, a woman with supernatural powers.

clue.text: Develop in the lab or at experimental section

indicators.note: in, with section, shows the answer lies within the run of words that follows
a section is a part cut from the run of words, so the answer is a stretch of the letters

explanation.surface: Scientists work up an idea in a laboratory trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' and 'section' point to the letters running from the end of 'the' to the start of 'experimental'.
explanation.definitionFit: To elaborate an idea is to work it out in more detail.

clue.text: Contradict opinion endlessly.

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter of the word for opinion is cut off

parts.note: a belief is an opinion firmly held

explanation.surface: Someone keeps on disputing a view without stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: To belie a claim is to show it to be false.

clue.text: Demonstrated limits of excellent fabric

parts.note: protesters who sat in staged a sit-in, a demonstration

indicators.note: limits are the edges, so take the first and last letters of excellent

explanation.surface: Someone showed off the edges of a fine cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrated' is a protest sense: SAT IN, as at a sit-in. 'limits of' takes E and T from 'excellent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Satinet is a thin imitation satin cloth.

clue.text: Viewer's outcry

parts.note: the viewer is a fox hunter who has just sighted the quarry and shouts to the pack

explanation.surface: Television watchers protest loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewer' suggests a TV audience complaining; in hunting, to view a fox is to sight it.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional shout of a huntsman on spotting a fox in British fox hunting.
